description:
Welcome to LunarEdge!

We are a team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, working on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge.

Our goal is to develop an interactive and user friendly platform that helps explore and compare potential lunar landing sites using NASA data.

You don't need to be an expert in everything. We value creativity, teamwork, curiosity, and a willingness to learn and build something meaningful together.

Let's help shape the future of lunar explore!
summary: LunarEdge is a web app for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. It catalogs six NASA/GSFC LOLA south pole regions, runs live JPL Horizons analysis for chosen UTC windows, and compares two sites on the same clock. Mission views show Sun/Earth geometry, charts, and operational windows; we label unknowns as N/A, not zero. The tool helps educators and planners explore south-pole illumination and Earth visibility trade offs. It is decision-support only not NASA endorsed or a certified landing safety product.
details:
How it works

LunarEdge is a browser app for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. Users choose from six NASA/GSFC LOLA 5 m/px south-pole regions (Product 78), pick a UTC time window, and run analysis on the Mission screen. The backend calls NASA JPL Horizons for topocentric Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation, returns time-series samples, and the frontend plots elevation charts, a local sky / horizon view, and operational window summaries (e.g. sunlight span and set behavior when the geometry supports it).

Compare runs the same UTC window for two catalogue sites so differences are not from mismatched clocks. Candidates shows catalogue facts and a south-pole map sketch. Sources documents NASA data links and our data honesty rules. An in-app tour explains flows and why N/A means unknown, not zero.

Architecture: Next.js UI → FastAPI REST API → Horizons; site metadata from Supabase (when configured) or a JSON catalogue fallback.

Benefits

  • Same-clock, site-to-site comparison for illumination and Earth line-of-sight at the south pole.
  • Live NASA ephemeris, not static screenshots—results change with site and dates the user selects.
  • Transparent limits: unverified or unavailable values stay N/A; we do not imply false precision or a “safest site” ranking.
  • Accessible to non-experts: visual charts and sky views plus links to Moon Trek and LROC QuickMap for deeper exploration.
  • Reproducible: analysis can be retrieved and exported (e.g. CSV) for sharing or follow-up.

Intended impact

Support educators, students, and early mission planners exploring Artemis-era south-pole trade space—how place and epoch affect power, thermal, and communications considerations—without replacing certified flight tools. Longer term, the pattern (catalogue + Horizons + honest UI) could extend to more sites, terrain context from LOLA products, and stronger validation workflows.

LunarEdge is decision-support only. It is not NASA-endorsed and does not certify landing safety.

Tools, languages, hardware, software

Area

Used

Languages

TypeScript, Python, SQL

Frontend

Next.js (App Router), React, Tailwind CSS, Recharts; custom SVG/canvas visualization

Backend

FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, HTTPX, NumPy

Data / APIs

JPL Horizons API; NASA GSFC PGDA Product 78 (site names/DEM metadata); optional Supabase (Postgres + RLS) for landing_sites

Dev / quality

ESLint, pytest, Ruff; Git

Hardware

Standard team laptops; no custom or embedded hardware

Deploy

Designed for hosted frontend (e.g. Vercel) and API backend with CORS; local dev on ports 3000 / 8000

How the project is creative

  • Visual-first navigation (Candidates → Mission → Compare) with short hints instead of long reports.
  • Integrity as UX: onboarding contrasts N/A vs “0 hours” so judges and users see we avoid misleading numbers.
  • Local sky and horizon views tied to the same Horizons samples as the charts—not a separate fake animation.
  • Compare as a product principle: one shared UTC window, two sites—optimized for fair debate, not a leaderboard.
  • Catalogue discipline: only documented GSFC sites, aligned with Product 78 naming—not invented landing locations.

Factors the team considered

  • Challenge fit: tie official LOLA landing-site products to time-varying Sun/Earth geometry via Horizons.
  • Scientific honesty: coordinates and altitude policy (e.g. altitude null until DEM-sampled); no invented metrics.
  • Scope for a hackathon: live ephemeris + compare + catalogue; bulk LOLA rasters and full terrain masking deferred.
  • Security & ops: no secrets in the frontend; CORS scoped to known origins; RLS on read-only public site data.
  • Audiences: quick demo for judges, clarity for students, enough rigor that numbers trace to Horizons and Product 78.
  • Team split: integration/API, dashboard UX, visualization, Horizons/parser/science backend—one shared API contract.
